Source: TODO.md

Features and design ideas to be considered for future releases.

Formalize the total-progress-budget-of-one contract

Each task is implicitly understood to have a total amount of 1 to “spend” across all of its calls to progressor(), e.g.

p(amount = 0)
p(amount = 0.5)
p(amount = 1)  # default

This has been the de facto design contract since the beginning, but it is not formally documented or validated anywhere. Consider:

  • Documenting this contract explicitly in ?progressor and the vignettes.
  • Optionally warning (opt-in?) if the cumulative amount reported by a progressor exceeds its allotted total, to help users catch bugs.

Allow a task to expand or shrink its number of steps

A task may not know its total number of steps up front, e.g. it discovers partway through that it needs to split into, say, five subtasks. There is currently no way to relay this back to the overall steps count used by progressor().

Idea: support something like

p(amount = 0, expand = +5)   # grow the total by 5 steps
...
p(amount = 0, expand = -3)   # later, shrink back down by 3 steps

Open questions:

  • How does expand interact with handlers() that have already rendered a progress bar with a fixed total (e.g. utils::txtProgressBar()), where the max value cannot easily be changed mid-flight?
  • Should expand be relative (+5/-3) as sketched above, or should there also be an absolute form (e.g. steps = 10)?
  • How should this be communicated through makeProgressionHandler() to existing handlers, i.e. does this require a new progression condition field (e.g. amount’s sibling expand), and how should handlers that are unaware of expand degrade gracefully?

Relay which task a sequence of progression updates belongs to

A single task often sends several progression updates over its lifetime, e.g. “I’ve started”, “I’m still running, +0.1 done”, …, “I’m done, here’s the remaining delta”:

p(amount = 0)                 # task has started
p(amount = 0.1)                # a few more steps done, still running
...
p(amount = remaining_delta)    # final update, closes out to amount = 1

Internally, each progression condition already carries a progressor_uuid (and owner_session_uuid) identifying which progressor() it came from, and a type field that distinguishes "initiate", "update", and "finish" (see R/progression.R and R/progressor.R). So the plumbing to tell updates apart by task already exists at the condition level. What appears to be missing:

  • A documented, user-facing way to get at this - e.g. can a handler or a downstream consumer easily tell “these three progression conditions all came from the same task” without reaching into internal/@keywords internal fields like progressor_uuid?
  • A human-readable task label/name (as opposed to an opaque UUID) that a caller could optionally set once (e.g. via progressor(..., label = "download")) and have carried on every subsequent p() call from that task, for handlers that want to render per-task status (started / running / done).
  • A convenience for the common “close out whatever is left” pattern, e.g. p(amount = NA) or similar meaning “add whatever amount is needed to bring this task’s cumulative total up to 1”, instead of requiring the caller to track and compute remaining_delta by hand.

Document how to gather and re-relay incoming progression conditions

There is currently no end-user or developer documentation on how to write a handler (or similar) that gathers incoming progression conditions and decides, on its own terms, how and when to relay them onward. A concrete use case: a handler sitting between many downstream progress updates (e.g. from nested futures) and the thing ultimately presenting progress, which only wants to relay, say, 1 out of every 100 collected updates upstream - either to reduce intrusiveness/ overhead, or because the upstream consumer can’t keep up.

Gathering is particularly useful for nested task structures. For example, 50 outer iterations each running 75 inner iterations produce 3,750 individual progress updates in total. Relaying every single one of those upstream (e.g. to a terminal progress bar, or across a future/cluster boundary) is both wasteful and more granular than any human-facing renderer needs; what matters upstream is typically a much coarser signal, e.g. one update per outer iteration, or one every 100 inner updates regardless of which outer iteration they belong to.

Prior art already in the package that is relevant here, but not tied together into guidance:

  • progressor() already has offset/scale/transform arguments (see R/progressor.R) for mapping an inner progressor’s step numbering into an outer progressor’s step space - this addresses nested step accounting, but not nested event volume. Even with steps correctly flattened/transformed, a 50x75 nested loop still signals 3,750 separate progression conditions; offset/scale/ transform don’t reduce that count, they just make the numbers line up.
  • make_progression_handler() already supports a time-based throttle via its interval/times/intrusiveness arguments (see R/make_progression_handler.R), which controls how often a handler renders, i.e. “no more often than every N seconds.” This is different from a count-based “every Nth update” throttle, which does not appear to exist.
  • with_progress() already talks about capturing and relaying conditions (delay_stdout, delay_conditions; see R/with_progress.R), which is close in spirit to “gather now, relay later” but is about stdout/other conditions around the progress session, not about re-batching the progression updates themselves.

Open questions / things to document or add:

  • Is there already a supported way to write a custom handler function (the handler argument to make_progression_handler()) that accumulates state across calls (e.g. a counter in a closure) and only forwards/renders every Nth update? If so, this should be written up as a worked example in a (new?) developer-facing vignette.
  • If no such mechanism exists, consider adding a built-in, reusable helper (e.g. a count-based analogue to interval, such as every = 100) to make_progression_handler() so handler authors don’t have to reimplement counting/batching logic themselves.
  • Clarify how “relaying upstream” is meant to work across session/ process boundaries (e.g. nested with_progress() calls, or progress from futures/workers bubbling up to the top-level session) versus just within a single handler instance.

Support structured, machine-readable progression messages

Related to the gather-and-relay idea above: a task’s progress message does not have to be a human-readable string. A framework could instead have tasks and subtasks send progression updates whose message encodes a small structured payload (e.g. a JSON object describing which subtask, what state, etc.). A gathering handler could then collect and parse these structured messages and summarize the result either by:

  • feeding the summary straight into its own renderer, or
  • signaling brand new, regular progression conditions (with plain, human-readable messages) that ordinary progressr handlers can consume as-is, i.e. using the gathering handler as a “translator”/aggregator layer in front of standard handlers.

Note that message is already documented as accepting “a character vector or a function” (see ?progression), and nothing in progression() itself coerces message to character at creation time - only conditionMessage.progression() does as.character(message) when rendering it (see R/progression.R). So, in principle, a structured object could already be stashed in message (e.g. as a closure returning a JSON string, or even as a list, as long as the handler consuming it knows to look past the default conditionMessage() coercion). This is, however, undocumented and unsupported as a design pattern. Consider:

  • Documenting (and testing) that message may carry structured, non-human-readable data for cases where the consuming handler knows how to interpret it, as opposed to always being, or coercing cleanly to, a display string.
  • Deciding whether structured payloads belong in message at all, versus being passed via the ... (additional named elements) of progression()/progressor(), which may be the more natural place for machine-readable, handler-specific metadata.
  • Providing a worked example (vignette and/or @examples) showing a custom handler that parses such structured updates from several (sub)tasks and re-signals a condensed, human-readable progression condition for consumption by standard handlers like handler_txtprogressbar() or handler_cli().

Caveat: a generic, open-ended “metadata” field is risky because progression conditions are not only consumed in-process - they may be serialized and relayed over channels progressr does not control (e.g. across future workers/clusters, or any other condition-forwarding mechanism). An arbitrarily large structured payload attached to every update could then blow up serialization size/time and network overhead for every single progress update, not just the ones that need it. progression objects already track this indirectly - print.progression() reports both the in-memory and serialized size of a condition (via serialization_size(); see R/progression.R) - so size-awareness is already a concern in the package, just not yet enforced or documented as a constraint for any future “carry structured metadata” feature. Any such feature should therefore:

  • Keep structured metadata strictly opt-in and caller-sized (i.e. the caller must decide to add it and keep it small), not a default or implicit part of every p() call.
  • Consider documenting/warning about (or even capping) payload size for any new metadata field, precisely because the sender cannot know in advance which handlers/channels a condition will be relayed through.
  • Favor designs where heavy payloads are summarized/reduced as early as possible (e.g. close to where they are generated, such as within a gathering handler on the same worker) rather than relayed upstream in full and only reduced once they reach a top-level handler.

Convey per-task success/failure/error/interrupted, not just completion

A progression update currently has no standard way to say how a task finished - only that it did. At the per-progressor() level, the "finish" type (see R/progressor.R) is signaled via on.exit() regardless of whether the enclosing call returned normally or exited via an error/interrupt - there is no type = "error" or type = "interrupted" counterpart at that level, so a handler cannot currently distinguish “this task’s progressor finished because the task succeeded” from “… because the task errored/was interrupted”.

Prior art that is close, but scoped differently:

  • with_progress() already detects an error or interrupt condition raised by its entire wrapped expression and signals a control_progression("interrupt", message = ...) to handlers (see handle_interrupt_or_error() in R/with_progress.R, and global_progression_handler.R), and make_progression_handler() already has a dedicated interrupt reporter slot that several handlers implement (e.g. handler_beepr(), handler_cli(), handler_txtprogressbar()). This is a whole-session level signal, though: it fires once, for the top-level with_progress(expr) call as a whole, not per task/subtask within it. For example, in a future_lapply() over 1,000 tasks where a handful of the tasks error out but the overall call still returns (e.g. errors are caught/collected per-element), today there is no progression signal distinguishing those failed tasks from the successful ones.

Open questions:

  • Should this be a new type value (e.g. "error") alongside the existing "initiate"/"update"/"finish"/"shutdown"/ "interrupt", or should "finish" gain a status field (e.g. status = c("success", "error", "interrupted")) carried alongside it?
  • How would a caller signal this in practice? e.g. would progressor()’s own on.exit()-based auto-finish need to detect whether it’s running during error unwinding (akin to base::on.exit(..., after = ...) or inspecting sys.on.exit()/condition handling at exit time), or would this need to be explicit, e.g. p(type = "error")/p(amount = 0, status = "error") called by the user’s own tryCatch()/try() around the task body?
  • How should existing handlers that don’t know about a new error/interrupted status degrade gracefully (e.g. just treat it as a normal "finish"), consistent with how unknown types/reporter slots are already ignored elsewhere in make_progression_handler()?

Related: a task may also finish early by its own choice rather than by error or interruption, e.g. an inner loop declared with steps = 75 decides after 43 steps that it’s done (converged, found what it was looking for, etc.) and deliberately stops - this is neither an error nor an interruption, it is a successful but early finish. This interacts with the budget-of-one contract and with steps/expand:

  • If amount/step are derived from the declared steps = 75, then stopping at step 43 leaves the task’s cumulative amount short of 1 - e.g. a txtprogressbar-style handler may be left showing “57% done” forever for that task’s slice of the bar, unless the early "finish" is itself treated as “jump straight to amount = 1” (similar to the “close out the remaining delta” idea in the task-identity section above).
  • Should an early, successful finish be distinguishable (e.g. for logging/summaries) from a finish that ran all declared steps? Or is it enough that, from the progress bar’s point of view, any "finish" simply means “fill this task’s slice to 100% and move on,” regardless of how many of the declared steps were actually used?

Signal “this task/step was skipped” (important for ETA estimation)

Separately from success/failure/early-finish above, it should be possible to signal that a task or step was skipped entirely, i.e. no real work was done for it (e.g. it was already cached, excluded by a filter, or a no-op). This matters specifically for ETA estimation:

progressr itself does not compute ETA - that is delegated to downstream renderers (e.g. cli’s cli::pb_eta, used by handler_cli(), or progress’s :eta, used by handler_progress(); see R/handler_cli.R and R/handler_progress.R), which estimate time remaining from elapsed time versus steps/amount completed so far - implicitly assuming roughly uniform work per step. A run of skipped steps completing “instantly” looks, to that kind of estimator, like the task sped up a lot, which skews the rate used to project ETA for the remaining, non-skipped work. The same problem applies to any custom gathering handler (see the gathering section above) that tries to compute its own throughput/ETA from collected updates.

Open questions:

  • Should this be a new type (e.g. "skip"), parallel to the "error"/"interrupted"/early-"finish" cases discussed above, so it’s really one broader “how did this update/task conclude” vocabulary rather than several one-off special cases?
  • A skipped task/step presumably still counts toward overall completion (the amount/steps total), it just shouldn’t count toward the rate used for ETA. Handlers and gathering layers need a way to tell these apart - does that mean the skip signal needs to be visible all the way down to whatever does the ETA math (e.g. passed through to cli/progress), or is it enough for a gathering handler to filter skipped updates out before computing its own rate/ETA and relaying a plain "update" upstream?
  • How should existing handlers that don’t recognize "skip" degrade (presumably: treat it just like a normal "update"/"finish", same as the graceful-degradation question raised above)?

Signal step state (started, running, finished, skipped, errored) in p() and render with distinct symbols and colors

The core API currently lacks a first-class way to signal the execution state of an individual step or task on each p() call. Today, p() accepts message, amount, class, and ... (see R/progressor.R), and while condition objects carry an internal type field ("initiate", "update", "finish", etc.; see R/progression.R), that field serves the condition-handling lifecycle rather than communicating the domain state of a unit of work.

If p() allows callers to explicitly declare state:

p(state = "started")    # or "running": work on this step/task has begun
...
p(state = "finished")   # completed successfully (default when amount > 0)
# or terminal alternatives:
p(state = "skipped")    # step bypassed (cached, filtered, no-op)
p(state = "errored")    # step failed with an error
p(state = "interrupted")# step was aborted

then progression handlers could use that rich information to render non-binary progress in the terminal and other interfaces.

Rendering multi-state progress bars

Progress bars traditionally treat steps as strictly binary: completed vs remaining (e.g. [========------------] 40%). With explicit step states, renderers can display multi-state bars that distinguish in-flight work from finished, skipped, or failed work using different characters, symbols, or ANSI colors:

  • In-flight / running steps: Represented using active symbols (e.g. >, ~, spinning glyphs |/-\) or accent colors (e.g. cyan, amber, blue).
  • Retrying / restarted steps: Represented using retry glyphs (e.g. ↻, >², or blinking/amber indicators) to highlight repeated work.
  • Finished steps: Represented using standard completion symbols (e.g. =, #, ✔) or green.
  • Skipped steps: Represented using dimmed or distinct symbols (e.g. -, s) or grey.
  • Errored / interrupted steps: Represented using alert symbols (e.g. !, ✖) or red.

Possible rendering layouts include:

  • Stacked / segmented bar: e.g. [====>>>↻!!s-----] 40% (4 finished, 3 in-flight, 1 retrying, 2 errored, 1 skipped, 5 pending).
  • Per-step glyph / array view: e.g. [✔✔✔▶▶↻!s··] for discrete step lists or worker status grids.
  • ANSI color-segmented bar: A continuous bar where completed, in-flight, retrying, errored, and skipped fractions are rendered with distinct background or foreground colors.

Lifecycle state machine: retries and restarts

In real-world distributed, network-bound, or fault-tolerant workflows, tasks may need to restart or retry. Examples include automatic retries upon transient HTTP or database errors, re-dispatching a future after a cluster node failure, spot-instance preemption, or a watchdog restarting a stalled worker.

This implies that step states do not merely follow a one-way progression from pending to a terminal state (finished/skipped/errored), but form a state machine supporting restarts and retries:

               +------------------+
               |     pending      |
               +------------------+
                        |
                        v
        +-------->   started   <---------+
        |               |                |
        | (restart)     v                | (retry)
        +---------   running             |
                     /  |  \             |
                    /   |   \            |
                   v    |    v           |
             finished   |   errored -----+
                        v
                   interrupted

Key state transitions to support:

  • running -> started: A task that was already in-flight resets or restarts from scratch (e.g. parameter divergence, watchdog reset).
  • errored -> started: A failed task is retried after catching an error (e.g. exponential backoff on network timeout).
  • interrupted -> started: A task that was cancelled or preempted is resumed or retried.

Visualizing concurrency and worker utilization

This is particularly impactful for parallel workflows (e.g. future with multiple background workers or cluster nodes):

  • Without a "started" signal, a progress bar only updates when tasks complete. While heavy computations run, the bar sits completely static, providing no visual indication of whether workers are active or stalled.
  • With p(state = "started") (or "running"), multiple concurrent tasks signal their start before finishing. Handlers can immediately show the number of actively computing workers (e.g. showing 8 > slots in flight across an 8-core cluster), giving users real-time feedback on worker concurrency and resource utilization.

Interactions with existing proposals

This proposal connects and unifies several related items in this file:

  • Convey per-task success/failure/error/interrupted, not just completion: Moves error and interrupt signaling from whole-session exception handling into the per-step state vocabulary.
  • Signal “this task/step was skipped”: Treats "skipped" as one of the standard step states alongside "finished" and "errored".
  • Relay which task a sequence of progression updates belongs to: Provides the task correlation needed so handlers know which "started" step matches a subsequent "finished" or "errored" update.

Open questions

  • API ergonomics & defaults:
    • Should state be a formal argument to progressor()’s returned function, e.g. p(amount = 1, state = c("finished", "started", "running", "skipped", "errored", "interrupted"))?
    • What should the default be when state is not specified? Calling p() with amount > 0 should default to state = "finished" for backward compatibility. Does p(state = "started") implicitly default to amount = 0 (marking a step in-flight without advancing the completed count)?
  • Retries, restarts & counter integrity:
    • If a task transitions errored -> started or running -> started, how do handlers adjust counts without double-counting in-flight steps? A naive counter (in_flight = started - finished - errored - skipped) would increment in_flight a second time unless the handler either maintains a per-task state table (keyed by progressor_uuid or slot index) or the update explicitly signals a restart/retry (e.g. p(state = "restarted") or p(state = "started", retry = TRUE)).
    • Budget-of-one reset/refund: If a task spent partial amount (e.g. p(amount = 0.4)) before failing or restarting, does transitioning back to started implicitly reset or refund that task’s spent amount back to 0? If a progress bar has already advanced to reflect that 0.4, does it visibly step backward upon restart, or does the handler hold progress until the retried task surpasses its previous point?
    • Impact on ETA estimation: Time spent on failed or restarted attempts produces no net progress. Should an ETA engine include that time in its overall throughput calculations (reflecting the real-world cost of retries), or should retried elapsed time be isolated to avoid skewing rate estimates for healthy tasks?
  • Slot tracking in handlers:
    • How should handlers track active in-flight steps? For aggregate segmented bars, a simple counter of in_flight = started - finished - errored - skipped may suffice. For per-step glyph arrays, handlers need a way to correlate start and stop events to a specific slot (e.g. via step index or task identity / UUID).
    • How should handlers handle out-of-order events or orphaned starts (e.g. if a worker crashes before signaling finish)?
  • Handler support & graceful degradation:
    • Existing handlers that only inspect progression$amount (e.g. utils::txtProgressBar()) will naturally ignore state and continue advancing only on completed amount, so p(state = "started") remains a safe no-op for unaware handlers.
    • Which handlers should natively implement multi-state rendering? handler_cli() and handler_txtprogressbar() could support configurable characters and ANSI colors for each state, and a specialized concurrency handler could display active worker slots.

A built-in ETA engine in progressr itself

As noted above, progressr currently does not compute ETA at all - it just forwards amount/step/time on each progression condition, and each handler’s underlying renderer (cli’s cli::pb_eta, progress’s :eta, etc.) does its own, independent rate-based ETA estimation from that. This means ETA quality and behavior differs per handler, every handler effectively re-implements the same amount-vs-elapsed-time math, and there’s no single place that could account for progressr-specific signals like "skip" updates (see above), nested tasks, or multiple concurrent progressors contributing to one overall ETA.

Idea: provide an ETA engine inside progressr that listens to all incoming progression updates (plausibly implemented as, or alongside, a “gathering” handler/layer - see the gathering section above) and itself produces ETA estimates, which it could then either expose for handler authors to use directly, or relay as new fields/conditions that any handler can pick up without having to implement its own rate estimation.

Open questions:

  • Where would this live - as a new built-in “reporter” field/API passed to handlers via make_progression_handler(), as a standalone helper handlers can opt into, or as part of with_progress()/the global progression handler itself?
  • What estimator should it use - a simple linear elapsed-time-per-completed-amount rate (like most existing renderers), a moving/exponentially-weighted average that adapts to changing rates, or something configurable? How would it combine estimates across multiple concurrent progressors (e.g. several parallel workers each with their own rate)?
  • How would it use "skip" updates (excluded from the rate calculation but still counted toward completion), early/partial finishes (see above), and expand/steps changes (see above) so the ETA doesn’t become wildly wrong when the denominator itself is moving?
  • Should this replace, or simply complement/feed into, the ETA already computed by downstream renderers like cli and progress? Fully replacing them would mean reimplementing functionality those packages already provide; just complementing them mainly helps handlers that don’t have their own ETA logic (e.g. handler_txtprogressbar()).
  • Should the computed ETA be exposed to handler authors as part of the existing state/config passed into reporter functions in make_progression_handler(), so handlers that want to display it don’t need to compute it themselves?

Audit laziness/consistency of how progressr.enable is ingested

(Prompted by documenting, in ?progressr.options and ?handlers, that handlers() only treats progressr.enable as read every time progress is reported - i.e. lazily - when handlers are specified by name or as unevaluated handler functions, e.g. handlers("txtprogressbar"). If a handler is instead passed already-called, e.g. handlers(handler_txtprogressbar()), the option is resolved once, at that call, and effectively locked in for that handler object’s lifetime.)

progressr.enable is not read in just one place; at least:

  • make_progression_handler() (R/make_progression_handler.R:98) reads it as a default for its own enable argument, falling back to interactive() if unset.
  • progressor() (R/progressor.R:66) independently reads it as a default for its own enable argument, falling back to TRUE (not interactive()) if unset - and, like the already-called-handler case above, this value is resolved once, at progressor() creation time, and baked into that progressor’s closure for its whole lifetime (see void_progressor in R/progressor.R, also referenced in the “Make p() a no-op when nothing is listening” section below).
  • handler_filesize(), handler_slowdown(), and handler_shiny() (R/handler_filesize.R:30, R/handler_slowdown.R:26, R/handler_shiny.R:32) each have their own enable = getOption("progressr.enable", TRUE) default, rather than deferring to make_progression_handler()’s default - also falling back to TRUE, not interactive().

So there are (at least) two axes of inconsistency:

  • When the option is resolved - lazily, on every progress event (string/name handlers, via as_progression_handler()), versus once and locked in (already-called handler objects; every progressor() call).
  • What the fallback default is when the option is altogether unset - interactive() in make_progression_handler(), but a hardcoded TRUE in progressor() and the three handler constructors above. (In practice, update_package_options() in R/options.R already sets progressr.enable to interactive() at package load time - see update_package_option("enable", ..., default = interactive()) around R/options.R:280 - so this divergence is currently masked for ordinary use; it would only surface if something explicitly unset the option again, e.g. options(progressr.enable = NULL).)

Open questions:

  • Should there be a single, canonical ingestion point for progressr.enable (e.g. only make_progression_handler() reads the option; progressor() and the three handler constructors above defer to it/a shared helper instead of each hardcoding their own getOption(...) default), so the two inconsistencies above collapse into one documented, single-sourced behavior?
  • Should ingestion always be lazy (resolved at the moment progress is actually about to be rendered/signaled), or is “baked in at construction time” actually the intended, documented contract for progressor() and already-called handler objects? Right now this reads as an accident of implementation (whether the default argument happens to be forced before or after the user next changes the option) rather than a deliberate design choice.
  • This directly matters for parallel/future workers: if ingestion becomes (or is clarified to already be) lazy end-to-end, then a worker process must never itself flip progressr.enable globally (e.g. options(progressr.enable = FALSE)) as a local optimization/side effect, since - on a persistent worker reused across multiple future() calls (e.g. multisession/cluster backends) - that would silently disable progress reporting for every subsequent, unrelated task dispatched to that same worker, not just the one that flipped it. This is a sharper version of the propagation gap already discussed in “Make p() a no-op when nothing is listening” below: that section is about master → worker propagation of progressr.enable; this is about the reverse direction - a worker’s own code must not be allowed to mutate that option persistently and leak the change across tasks/sessions it doesn’t own.

Make p() a no-op when nothing is listening

Investigate whether the function returned by progressor() (what users call as p()) can cheaply become a true no-op whenever there is no progress handler actually listening - not just when the user explicitly disabled progress via enable = FALSE.

There is already a related mechanism to build on: when enable = FALSE (controlled by the progressr.enable option), progressor() immediately returns a prebuilt void_progressor <- function(...) NULL instead of constructing a real progressor (see R/progressor.R). But enable defaults to TRUE and is a static choice made once, at progressor() creation time - it says nothing about whether the call actually happens inside an active with_progress() session (or under a manually registered handler via register_global_progression_handler()). In the common case of a package that unconditionally sprinkles p() calls through a tight loop, but whose caller never wrapped the call in with_progress(), every single p() call today still: increments progression_index, builds a full progression condition object (structure() with ~15 fields, including a session_uuid() lookup and timestamp formatting; see progression() in R/progression.R), and runs it through withRestarts(signalCondition(cond), ...) - all for a condition that, with nothing listening, is immediately discarded. That construction cost, not the (cheap) signalCondition() itself, is the overhead worth eliminating for tight loops.

There is also already a notion of a dynamic “is a handler currently active” state elsewhere in the package - see the active flag inside global_progression_handler() in R/global_progression_handler.R, which with_progress() toggles off/on around its own global handler registration. Something similar, but exposed cheaply enough to check on every p() call, is what this idea needs.

Open questions:

  • R has no built-in, cheap way to ask “is there a calling handler installed for condition class progression?” without actually signaling a condition. Any detection would have to be via progressr’s own bookkeeping (e.g. a package-level flag flipped by with_progress()/register_global_progression_handler() on enter/exit), not a general R introspection mechanism - so this can only ever detect “no progressr-managed session is active,” not “literally nobody is listening” (a user could always install their own withCallingHandlers(expr, progression = ...) directly, outside with_progress(), which progressr could not see).
  • False negatives (treating a call as a no-op when something was actually listening) would silently drop real progress updates, so any such flag must fail safe (default to “assume someone might be listening”) whenever its state is ambiguous, e.g. across process/ worker boundaries where futures run detached from the main session’s with_progress() state.
  • Would switching between “real” and “no-op” behavior need to happen per-p()-call (cheap flag check every time) or could a progressor that starts with nobody listening simply stay a no-op for its whole lifetime (and vice versa), trading a bit of responsiveness (a progressor created just before with_progress() starts wouldn’t “wake up”) for simplicity?
  • How much does this actually save in practice? Worth profiling progression()’s construction cost (object allocation, session_uuid(), timestamp formatting) in a tight loop before investing in the detection machinery, to confirm the payoff is worth the added complexity and the risk of silently-dropped updates above.

A concrete mechanism for the “how to detect it” question above: have the calling environment (i.e. with_progress(), which already knows whether it actually installed any handlers) query and record “is a listener active,” and broadcast that as a plain R option, which any nested progressor() call - including one created inside a future dispatched to a worker - can just read via getOption(). This is already largely in place for the plain, single-process case: ?with_progress documents that enabling/disabling is controlled by the progressr.enable option (or the R_PROGRESSR_ENABLE environment variable), and with_progress() concretely sets options(progressr.enable = enable) for the duration of its call (see R/with_progress.R, around where options[["progressr.enable"]] <- enable is assigned and then applied via options(options)). Every progressor() call already defaults its own enable argument to getOption("progressr.enable", TRUE) (see R/progressor.R), so a function called from inside an active with_progress() block already inherits “yes, enabled” (or “no, disabled”) through this option without any extra plumbing - as long as it runs in the same R process.

Where this idea adds something new is the future/worker boundary: options() set in the main session are not automatically copied into a separate future worker process (e.g. multisession/cluster backends start with their own, independent option defaults), so a progressor() created inside a future body currently falls back to getOption("progressr.enable", TRUE) as evaluated in the worker, not as it was in the master session that actually knows whether anyone is listening. (Note: a progressor created in the master and merely used inside a future already sidesteps this, since its enable value is baked into the closure at creation time and travels with it as part of the future’s exported globals - this gap is specifically about progressors created fresh inside worker code.)

Open questions specific to this mechanism:

  • Would propagating progressr.enable (and perhaps other progress-relevant options) to workers need to piggyback on future’s own globals-export mechanism (e.g. via future::plan() options, or future.globals), or would progressr need its own hook into future (e.g. something run at the start of every future expression) to copy the option across?
  • Is a single boolean option enough, or does “is a listener active” need to be richer - e.g. which handlers, with what interval/ times settings - so a worker-side progressor can make the same no-op decision a master-side one would?
  • This would need to stay consistent with the “fail safe” principle above: if propagation itself fails or is skipped (e.g. an unsupported future backend), the worker-side default must remain “assume enabled,” not silently go quiet.

This whole idea is already on record, in more detail than the above, as two still-open upstream issues:

  • futureverse/progressr#2 (“PERFORMANCE: Avoid progress updates if no one is listening”) and futureverse/progressr#155 (“Detect registered progress handler”) discuss a “confirm”/handshake design: a publisher signals a progression carrying a confirm callback, and a listening handler calls it back (then invokeRestart("muffleProgression")), so the publisher learns someone is there without a separate side channel. #2 explicitly raises the future/worker case: “the relaying of conditions by the future framework: when future collects conditions = 'progression' … the publisher needs a way to know that it will not receive a confirmation in this case. For the latter, maybe this can be done via a global R option which is set for some of the future backends … but not others?” - i.e. the exact option-based mechanism sketched above. #155 separately proposes a simpler boolean check (has_progressr_handlers() / progression_handler_exists()), and notes a real caution from the maintainer’s own prior answer: a package should not change its own internal behavior (e.g. a task-splitting strategy) based on whether progress is enabled, since the user may have turned on a global handler for reasons unrelated to that package.
  • The future/worker half of this is also blocked on a longstanding, still-open gap in future itself, not something progressr can solve unilaterally: futureverse/future#134 (“R options: options() are not passed down to futures - should they?”, open since 2018) establishes that R’s global options() are not automatically copied into future workers at all (only a few future.globals.* options got special-cased in future 1.9.0); the documented workaround is always to manually snapshot options into a global and restore them inside the future body. A concrete, still-open proposal to fix this generally is futureverse/future#480, which would add a future(..., options = c("foo", BAR = 42L)) (and envvars =) argument for explicit, per-call option passing. Henrik’s own stated design reasoning there favors this explicit, opt-in approach over silently/automatically forwarding everything, since not all future backends can set options on their workers - the same fail-safe/opt-in principle noted above. Any progressr.enable-to-worker propagation should probably build on future#480’s mechanism if/when it lands, rather than progressr inventing its own separate propagation channel.

A more targeted alternative to both of the above: a future_meta convention on the future side (tracked in ~/futureverse/future/TODO.md) where a function can declare, via an attribute on the function itself, extra options that should be forwarded to the worker whenever that function is referenced by a future expression. This is specifically aimed at the gap identified above - a fresh progressor() call made inside worker-executed code (e.g. code injected by progressify()), which today resolves enable from getOption("progressr.enable", TRUE) as evaluated in the worker, with no knowledge of what the master session had set.

The metadata has to sit on the exported generator function progressr::progressor itself, not on the closure it returns - a returned progressor’s no-op-ness is already permanently decided by the time it exists, so annotating it is too late to change anything. The generator’s attribute doesn’t need to be shipped anywhere either: it’s part of the installed progressr package, so it’s already present, identically, on any worker that attaches the package. All future needs to do is: when its existing globals/packages analysis of a future expression notices that progressor is referenced (which it already must do today, to know the worker needs the progressr package attached), also check for this metadata, snapshot getOption("progressr.enable") from the master, and arrange for it to be set on the worker (e.g. an auto-generated options(progressr.enable = <value>) prologue) before the expression runs. Then a fresh progressor() call on the worker resolves enable to the master’s actual value and correctly becomes void_progressor there too, with zero per-call-site annotation from the end user or from progressr callers. This idea is entirely blocked on future adopting the future_meta mechanism at all - it does not exist yet.

Update (2026-10-12): the attribute-on-a-function architecture this needs already has a close relative on the futureverse roadmap - the resources mechanism (https://www.futureverse.org/roadmap/resources.html, https://www.jottr.org/2026/08/11/roadmap-resources-memory/), which sets attr(fcn, "resources") via resources(fcn) <- function(...) ... and is consulted automatically by futurize(). So far it’s scoped to compute resources (memory, walltime, GPU), not packages/globals/ options, but extending it to cover this case is probably preferable to future inventing a separate future_meta attribute from scratch. See ~/futureverse/future/TODO.md and future-ideas#1117 for the fuller writeup, including how progressr itself would declare options = "progressr.enable" package-wide (not per-function): attach resources to progressr’s own .onLoad() as the default convention (no new API or file format needed), with a Config/future/options DESCRIPTION field or a load-free sidecar file as later, opt-in optimizations only for packages that want to avoid the namespace-load cost of inspecting .onLoad().

Caveat (worked out in more detail in ~/futureverse/future/TODO.md): per-function detection like the above has a real blind spot for nested futures whose existence/body is only constructed dynamically at runtime (as opposed to being lexically nested in the outer future’s literal source) - there is nothing for any ancestor’s static analysis to find in advance in that case, so the forwarded value never reaches the level where it’s actually needed. The more robust version of this idea moves the trigger from “is progressor referenced in this specific expression” to “is the progressr package currently loaded in my session” (checked via loadedNamespaces(), not search(), since progressify()-generated code would plausibly call progressr::progressor() without ever attaching the package) - a session-level fact that’s far more likely to already hold at every nesting level than a per-expression textual reference. This still needs future to implement that check independently of its existing packagesOf(globals)-based package-forwarding pipeline, since that pipeline is itself gated by the same static per-expression detection and wouldn’t otherwise provide the improvement for free.
